cues.text: A Scholar-Bishop of European Reputation
Born in 1469 at Beverley in Yorkshire, John Fisher studied at Cambridge, where his evident learning and piety drew Margaret Beaufort ’s attention.
Mother of King Henry VII, she made him her confessor and generous patron of scholarship at the university.
Fisher was appointed Bishop of Rochester in 1504, traditionally the poorest and least prestigious English see.
Unusually for an ambitious churchman of his era, Fisher chose to remain there for the rest of his life rather than seek advancement to a wealthier diocese.
He also served for decades as Chancellor of Cambridge University, working closely with Lady Margaret to establish new colleges and scholarships.
At one point, he acted as tutor to the young Prince Henry, the future Henry VIII, forming an early relationship that would turn, decades later, to bitter conflict.
A Defender Against Lutheranism
Fisher's international reputation as a theologian grew substantially through the 1520s, when he emerged as one of the most formidable Catholic controversialists.
He wrote against the spreading teachings of Martin Luther, producing scholarship of sufficient weight and rigor to earn him respect even among continental theologians who never met him in person.
Fisher's learning was considered so great that he was invited to preach the funeral orations for both King Henry VII and Lady Margaret Beaufort.
They died within months of each other in 1509, and the sermons are still studied today for their eloquence.
Standing Alone Among the Bishops

When Henry VIII sought to divorce Catherine of Aragon and eventually declared himself Supreme Head of the Church of England , Fisher emerged as one of the fiercest and most consistent defenders of the queen's marriage and papal authority.
This stand placed him in direct, escalating conflict with the king he had once personally tutored.
As one by one the English bishops yielded to mounting royal pressure and accepted the new order, Fisher stood essentially alone in his outright refusal.
He was a solitary conscience among an entire national episcopate that had, with only his exception, bent to the crown's demands.
A Cardinal's Hat in Prison

Imprisoned in the Tower of London in 1534 for refusing the Oath of Succession, Fisher endured over a year of harsh confinement, his health seriously deteriorating under the conditions of his imprisonment.
In a gesture that only inflamed Henry's fury, Pope Paul III created the imprisoned Fisher a cardinal in 1535.
He intended the honor as a mark of solidarity.
Henry reportedly responded that he would send Fisher's head to Rome instead of a hat for it to sit on.
Execution and a Rare English Isolation

Fisher was tried and convicted of treason on manufactured grounds and beheaded on Tower Hill on June 22, 1535, just two weeks before his friend Thomas More suffered the same fate for the same fundamental refusal.

His body was buried without ceremony, and his head, like More's, was displayed publicly on London Bridge before being removed, a fate the two old friends and fellow prisoners had, in their final months, quietly prepared each other to accept.
Legacy
Fisher's death, following so closely upon his elevation to the cardinalate, sent shockwaves through Catholic Europe and hardened continental opposition to Henry's religious policies.
Canonized together with Thomas More in 1935, John Fisher remains a uniquely solitary figure among the English martyrs of the Reformation.
He was the only bishop of the entire Catholic hierarchy in England who refused the king's supremacy to the end, a conscience that stood genuinely and almost entirely alone.
His isolation among his own brother bishops makes his final, costly fidelity all the more striking a witness to the whole Church that came after him.
A scholar who had once tutored the very king who condemned him, Fisher's example continues to remind every bishop that genuine episcopal courage is sometimes asked of exactly one man at a time.
